title: HPDT Phys21/525P — Ms Y (Physiotherapists)
text:
BEFORE THE HEALTH PRACTIONERS DISCIPLINARY TRIBUNAL
TARAIPUINARA WHAKATIKA KAIMAHI HAUORA
HPDT No: 1191/Phys 21/525P
UNDER the Health Practitioners Competence
Assurance Act 2003 (“the Act”)
IN THE MATTER of a disciplinary charge laid against a
health practitioner under Part 4 of the Act
BETWEEN A PROFESSIONAL CONDUCT COMMITTEE
appointed by the PHYSIOTHERAPY
BOARD OF NEW ZEALAND
Applicant
AND Ms Y of X, registered physiotherapist
Practitioner
Hearing: On the papers
Tribunal: Ms T M Baker (Chair)
Representation: Ms A Lane for the Professional Conduct Committee
Mr H Waalkens QC for the Practitioner
___________________________________________________________________________
WITHDRAWAL OF CHARGE AND ORDER FOR NAME SUPPRESSION

[1] In a Notice of Charge dated 20 July 2021, a Professional Conduct Committee (PCC)
appointed by the Physiotherapy Board of New Zealand alleged [Ms Y] was guilty of
professional misconduct under sections 100(1)(a) and/or (b) of the Health Practitioners
Competence Assurance Act 2003 (the Act). In particular it was alleged that she had entered
into a sexual relationship with a patient, provided physiotherapy treatment to someone with
whom she was in a close personal relationship and claimed payment from ACC for treatment
of someone with whom she was in a close personal relationship, contrary to ACC’s funding
requirements and policy statement.
[2] At a pre-hearing conference on 20 August 2021 no directions were made for the filing
of evidence or setting a hearing date. The parties indicated that an application might be made
for the charge to be withdrawn.
[3] In a joint application dated 2 September 2021 the parties have sought leave to
withdraw the charge. The parties have since agreed that although many of the previous
decisions to withdraw have been made by a panel of the Tribunal, I may make a decision as
Chair on my own. I note that unlike some cases where a charge has been withdrawn after
evidence has been filed and a panel selected to hear the charge, the present charge has only
just been laid. It would involve further expense and delay to convene a panel of the Tribunal,
not to hear a charge, but to decide whether it should be withdrawn. For the PCC, Ms Lane
submitted that a Chair alone may make the decision under Clause 5 of the First Schedule to
the Act, which allows the Tribunal to regulate its own procedure. She cited Nur08/88P as an
example of a Chair granting leave to withdraw a charge.
[4] The basis for the present application is that since the charge was laid, further
information has become apparent that is relevant to whether there is a public interest in the
charge against Ms Y being heard. In particular, the parties note the unique circumstances of
Ms Y’s relationship with Mr S and further information has come to light that is relevant to the
charge, including that Ms Y is [ ].
[5] The parties consider that any public interest issues that arise from the circumstances
that led to the charge have or will be dealt with in the following ways:
2

(a) Since the events that have given rise to the charge, Ms Y has completed a Post
Graduate Certificate in Rehabilitation and the Mental Health Education and
Resource Centre (MHERC) course on Boundaries and Ethics in Health and
Community Settings.
(b) The Physiotherapy Board has made enquiries into Ms Y’s competence and the
parties understand that the Board will consider that matter at its September
meeting.
Discussion
[6] As the Tribunal observed in Director of Proceedings v L (687/Mid14/276D):
In considering an application for leave to withdraw a charge, the Tribunal must be satisfied
that the parties have no sound objections to that course of action and that there are no
outstanding public interest issues that ought to be the subject of inquiry by the Tribunal
notwithstanding the attitude or agreement of the parties in the matter. The Tribunal has the
obligation under sections 85 and 100 of the Health Practitioners Competence Assurance Act
2003 to conduct a hearing and hear charges laid. One fact that ought to be taken into account
when leave is sought to withdraw a charge is that it is unlikely there will be any evidence called
by the party laying the charge or perhaps any other party and that the initiative for furthering
the hearing would lie with the Tribunal and this has its own practical implications.
[7] In the present case, it is puzzling that the practitioner’s personal circumstances were
not known to the PCC at the time the charge was laid. There are strong public interest factors
in charges of this nature in the maintenance of standards for the profession, not only in
relation to professional boundaries and ethics, but also the obligations of practitioners
receiving funding for services.
[8] However, given the personal circumstances of the practitioner and patient, there do
not appear to be any underlying concerns about patient safety, such that the Tribunal would
take the unusual step of insisting that the matter proceed.
[9] Leave is therefore granted for the PCC to withdraw the charge.
[10] The PCC also consents to orders prohibiting the publication of:
(a) the name of the practitioner, [Ms Y], and/or any details that may identify her;
3

(b) the name of the practitioner’s husband, [Mr S], and/or any details that may
identify him;
(c) the name of the practitioner’s employer, [ ], or details that might identify it;
(d) the place where the events the subject of this disciplinary charge occurred – [ ];
and
(e) the sport with which the matters the subject of the disciplinary charge concerned,
which is “[ ]”.
[11] Section 95 of the Act provides that every hearing of the Tribunal must be held in public
unless the Tribunal orders otherwise. In considering whether to prohibit publication of any
matter under section 95(2), the Tribunal must assess whether it is desirable to make any such
orders after considering:
(a) the interests of any person (which may include the complainant and/or the
practitioner and/or any third parties); and
(b) the public interest.
[12] The parties agree that there is no public interest in naming Ms Y (on the basis that
leave is granted to withdraw the charge). The parties refer to an earlier decision in Re T
(70/Med06/41D) where the Tribunal agreed that there is no public interest in naming a
practitioner where the charge has been withdrawn unless there are public safety issues. The
parties agree that there are no public safety issues in the present case.
[13] There has been no publicity of the facts that are the subject matter of the charge. The
practitioner’s personal interest in having her name suppressed outweigh any public interest
in knowing that a charge was laid and then withdrawn. It is therefore desirable to order under
section 95(2) of the Act, non-publication of the matters set out in paragraph 10 above.
4

[14] Unless either party wishes to be further heard, the directions conference set down for
Wednesday 22 September 2021 is vacated.
DATED at Wellington this 20th day of September 2021
…………………………….
T M Baker
Chair
Health Practitioners Disciplinary Tribunal
5
